problem: The range of the signature is written "0 ≤ s e mod n", which is not a valid condition and mixes the range with the public exponent. A student will read it as s·e mod n and not as the size limit on s.
fix: Write: "s is the signature, an integer with 0 ≤ s < n, where e is the public exponent."

where: Section 2 and Section 3, formulas inside running text
problem: Exponents are not marked up in the prose: "s = hd mod n", "(hd)e = hde", "se mod n", "s1 = h1d mod n", "(s1 s2)e = h1 h2 mod n" all read as multiplication. The failure is worst in Section 3, where the multiplication step looks like it follows from s1·s2·e = h1·h2, which is false.
fix: Use <sup> as in the formula block: s = h<sup>d</sup> mod n, (h<sup>d</sup>)<sup>e</sup> = h<sup>de</sup> = h mod n, s<sup>e</sup> mod n, s<sub>1</sub> = h<sub>1</sub><sup>d</sup> mod n, and (s<sub>1</sub>s<sub>2</sub>)<sup>e</sup> = h<sub>1</sub>h<sub>2</sub> mod n.

problem: The sentence ends "...and a valid signature, any message", which contradicts the definition just given: in an existential forgery the attacker does not get to pick the message.
fix: "An existential forgery produces at least one new message together with a valid signature for it; the attacker does not choose that message."

problem: The answer says "Existential: any new valid pair", which by the word "any" describes a universal forgery, the opposite of the intended meaning.
fix: "Existential: the attacker produces some new message with a valid signature, not a message of their choosing. Universal: the attacker can produce a valid signature for any message they are given or choose."

problem: The inverse k⁻¹ exists only if gcd(k, p − 1) = 1; the text says only to use a safe random k, which is too vague for a scheme where the modulus of the inverse is p − 1 and not a prime.
fix: Add: "k is chosen with 1 ≤ k ≤ p − 2 and gcd(k, p − 1) = 1, so that k⁻¹ mod (p − 1) exists."
